\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Lenders can send only a fixed share of loan applications to human
underwriters, so the deferral rule that selects those cases decides what the
review capacity is worth. We audit this rule in CredDefer, a deployed
credit-decisioning prototype evaluated on 307{,}511 real loan applications.
The audit is a permutation test that costs a few lines of code: compare the
deferred pile against 10{,}000 random routers at the same review rate. It
caught our production rule routing the model's most confident cases to
review (empirical $p < 10^{-4}$), traced the fault to a calibration offset
between two scores, and validated a repair that now runs as the production
default. On an untouched final split the repaired router cuts auto-decision
cost from 0.0729 to 0.0482 per applicant at the mandated 22.5\% review rate.
Epistemic uncertainty from a single boosted model routes review cases to
0.40 on a random-to-oracle scale against 0.14 for the classical reject
option, and a replication on a Taiwanese credit corpus transports the audit
while the best routing signal changes with the base rate. The audit
procedure, not any one signal, is the portable result.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
credit risk, learning to defer, human-in-the-loop, uncertainty quantification,
selective prediction, fairness, explainable AI
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
Automated credit assessment concentrates research attention on ranking
accuracy (AUC), while the institutions that deploy such models are
accountable for an entire decision process: which applications are decided
instantly, which are escalated to a human underwriter, what the applicant is
told, and what trail an auditor can follow. The operational problem of
allocating a fixed, scarce human-review capacity, and of verifying that a
deployed deferral rule actually does its job, has received far less
attention than the classifier itself. In India this accountability is
becoming explicit: the Reserve Bank of India's Digital Lending
Directions~\cite{rbi2025} and its FREE-AI committee report~\cite{rbifreeai}
expect explainable decisions, human oversight of uncertain cases, and
end-to-end auditability.

This paper reports the design and measured evaluation of CredDefer, a
human-in-the-loop credit decisioning prototype built and deployed on
307{,}511 real loan applications from the public Home Credit
corpus~\cite{homecredit}. Two framing points up front. First, the data is a
European lender's public dataset, not Indian lending data; we use Indian
regulatory framing because it is the deployment context we design for, and
all cost parameters are literature values, not measured portfolio
quantities. Second, two accuracy numbers recur in this paper and must not be
read as one comparison: the live serving model scores 0.6919 on its own
15-field holdout because it is deliberately restricted to the fields the
application form collects, while the best offline research model scores
0.7868 on the full feature frame; the gap is a serve-time contract choice,
not a modelling failure.

Our contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A permutation audit for deployed deferral rules, the inversion
it caught, and the measured repair.} A plausible-looking rule can silently
invert, and aggregate metrics do not show it. Our deployed disagreement rule
deferred the model's most confident cases; the audit exposed this with
10{,}000 permutations (empirical $p$-values to $10^{-4}$), the diagnosis
traced it to a calibration offset, and the repaired router survived a
three-stage split whose final slice no candidate ever saw. The repair now
runs as the production default (Sec.~\ref{sec:deferral}).
\item \textbf{A comparison of routing signals under one review budget.}
Knowledge uncertainty from a single stochastic-gradient Langevin boosted
model~\cite{ustimenko2021,malinin2021} reaches routing position 0.40 on a
random-to-oracle scale against 0.14 for the classical reject
option~\cite{chow1970}, without a second model; expected-loss ranking, not
uncertainty, minimises decision cost at the same budget; and a replication
on an independent Taiwanese corpus~\cite{yeh2009} shows the best uncertainty
signal changes with the base rate. The procedure transports; the signal does
not (Sec.~\ref{sec:deferral}).
\item \textbf{A measured subgroup account of who gets deferred.} The
thin-file deferral asymmetry is a property of the router: 3.4$\times$ under
the inverted rule, near-flat under the epistemic signal. We report approval,
calibration and ranking gaps per group as measurements
(Sec.~\ref{sec:fairness}).
\end{enumerate}

All supporting modelling claims were adjudicated by one pre-specified
fold-paired criterion, fixed in advance and committed with timestamps
(Sec.~\ref{sec:protocol}).

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
\textbf{Learning to defer.} Madras et al.\ framed deferral as joint
optimisation of a predictor and a rejector~\cite{madras2018}; consistent
surrogate losses and multi-expert extensions
followed~\cite{mozannar2020,mao2023}, deferral under congestion has been
analysed game-theoretically~\cite{lykouris2024}, and recent work treats the
rejector as an uncertain component via conformal prediction~\cite{fang2026}.
Studies of humans working with erroneous algorithmic scores document both
the value and the fragility of human override
behaviour~\cite{dearteaga2020}. We do not train a deferral policy jointly:
our setting is post-hoc and budget-constrained. The institution fixes the
classifier and a review capacity, and the question is which routing signal
deserves that capacity and how to verify the deployed rule. A learned
deferral or conformal baseline under the same budget is a fair ask and is
left as an explicit author decision for the next revision.

\textbf{Uncertainty and selective prediction.} Deep
ensembles~\cite{lakshminarayanan2017} estimate epistemic uncertainty;
calibration of modern models is fragile~\cite{guo2017}. For gradient-boosted
trees, SGLB~\cite{ustimenko2021} yields principled virtual ensembles from a
single model~\cite{malinin2021}, the mechanism we adopt. Conformal
prediction supplies distribution-free abstention
triggers~\cite{angelopoulos2023}; selective classification studies the
risk-coverage trade-off~\cite{geifman2017}, our yardstick in
Fig.~\ref{fig:riskcov}. Jones et al.\ show selective classification can
magnify group disparities~\cite{jones2021}, motivating
Sec.~\ref{sec:fairness}.

\textbf{Explainability.} SHAP~\cite{lundberg2017} and LIME~\cite{ribeiro2016}
dominate instance-level attribution in credit scoring; counterfactual
explanations supply recourse~\cite{wachter2017}. CredDefer adds a structural
guarantee: monotonicity constraints make the direction of key explanations a
model property rather than a post-hoc estimate (Sec.~\ref{sec:studies}).

\textbf{Tabular foundation models.} TabPFN performs in-context tabular
prediction~\cite{hollmann2025,tabpfn25}; Google's TabFM provides zero-shot
prediction~\cite{tabfm2026}; RealMLP~\cite{holzmuller2024} and
TabICLv2~\cite{qu2026} are strong recent baselines. We evaluate these
against tuned gradient boosting~\cite{chen2016,ke2017,prokhorenkova2018}
under one protocol (Sec.~\ref{sec:results}).

\section{System and Evaluation Protocol}\label{sec:protocol}

\subsection{System design}
Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} shows the pipeline. Four roles are kept separate: a
predictive model estimates default probability; CBES, a transparent rule
engine, supplies a domain-policy score; the decision layer combines the two
under thresholds and a capacity constraint; and the explanation layer
(per-decision SHAP, CBES pillar breakdowns, monotone reason directions)
communicates why.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_architecture.pdf}
\caption{The CredDefer pipeline. Two opinions (the calibrated serving model
and the CBES rule engine) are blended; the blend decides instantly outside
an uncertainty band and defers inside it. The serving model is deliberately
simpler than the offline research models of Sec.~\ref{sec:results}; the two
tracks are versioned separately. Every decision carries engine version,
artifact name and a threshold-artifact hash; reviewer outcomes are captured
behind a closed relearning gate with a 3\% exploration arm.}
\label{fig:arch}
\end{figure}

The serving model is a calibrated logistic regression over a 15-field
profile contract (holdout AUC 0.6919); the contract guarantees the
training-time feature derivation is byte-identical to the live API's. CBES
(Credit Behaviour Evaluation Score) is a rule engine over five weighted
pillars (credit 0.35, capacity 0.30, behaviour 0.20, stability 0.10, region
0.05), each passed through a softened logistic link and calibrated to a
probability. Its standalone AUC is 0.5650 on the full out-of-fold
population. It is retained because an all-ML pipeline fails two
institutional tests: a reviewer cannot argue with a gradient, and a
regulator cannot inspect one. Every pillar sub-score is shown to the
reviewer, so disagreement between the two opinions is itself interpretable.
CBES also enters the decision blend, so it is a bounded decision signal and
not only an explanation; Sec.~\ref{sec:studies} measures what that costs
and buys.

Decisions use $p = (1-\alpha)\,p_{ml} + \alpha\,p_{cbes}$ with
$\alpha = 0.10$ chosen from a cost table on a tuning split, bounding CBES's
influence to $\pm 0.0075$ in probability. The base approve threshold
($t_{base}=0.65$) is fitted by expected-cost minimisation, never on
evaluation data; approve and reject cutoffs bracket it, and the band between
them defers. The deferral rate is a business constraint (20--25\%
underwriter capacity; we operate at 22.5\%), implemented as a tuning-split
quantile of the deferral signal. Since 13 November 2026 the production
default routing signal is the repaired uncertainty rule of
Sec.~\ref{sec:deferral}, with the engine version bumped at the switch so
capture rows from the two routers stay separable.

Reviewer decisions, reason codes, self-rated confidence and handling time
are captured for governance analyses, but no code path reads them as
training labels: a four-condition relearning gate is evaluated on every
inspection and has never opened, and a 3\% exploration arm preserves the
counterfactual labels any future relearning would require. Training on
labels selected by one's own router is the selective-labels
problem~\cite{lakkaraju2017}, and the closed gate is our defence against
it. This is a deployed workflow prototype with reviewer-outcome capture; no
human-subject evaluation of reviewer decision quality has been conducted.
Every decision is stamped with the engine version, serving-artifact name,
and a hash of the threshold artifact.

\subsection{Evaluation protocol}
All experiments share one discipline, fixed in each experiment script's
header and committed before results existed. Data: the Home Credit
application table (307{,}511 rows, 8.07\% default rate; 14.3\% of
applicants are thin-file, meaning they have no credit-bureau record) plus
the credit-bureau table~\cite{homecredit}.

Three evaluation populations are never mixed. (A)~The main benchmark:
5-fold stratified cross-validation (seed 42) on all 307{,}511 rows,
identical folds across every experiment so deltas are fold-paired. (B)~The
foundation-model population: 8{,}000 rows joined by applicant identity with
an alignment gate (zero label mismatches). (C)~The serving evaluation: the
15-field contract's stratified holdout and the decision artifact built from
out-of-fold predictions. Results tables state their population.

For candidate $B$ and incumbent $A$ on identical folds $k = 1,\dots,5$ with
per-fold AUCs $a_k^{B}, a_k^{A}$, a gain counts only if
\begin{equation}
\tfrac{1}{5}\textstyle\sum_k \big(a_k^{B}-a_k^{A}\big) > 0.0036
\quad\text{and, for feature claims,}\quad a_k^{B} > a_k^{A}\;\forall k ,
\label{eq:claim}
\end{equation}
where $\pm0.0036$ is the observed fold-to-fold AUC standard deviation. This
is a pre-specified practical effect-size criterion, not a significance
test; five folds are not independent experiments. Where a claim matters we
also report paired-bootstrap confidence intervals on out-of-fold
predictions. These row-level intervals are conditional on the fitted
predictions: they quantify evaluation noise given the trained models, not
variability over retraining. Policy quantities (thresholds, calibrators,
deferral cutoffs) are fitted on a 50/50 tuning split (seed 20260831) and
reported on the held-out half. We use ROC-AUC as the model criterion
because at an 8\% default rate accuracy is dominated by the class prior
(always-approve scores 91.9\%). Table~\ref{tab:params} lists every
decision-layer quantity and how it was fitted; none is fitted on evaluation
data. One cost pair is used throughout the main text: false approval 0.45
(the Basel II F-IRB supervisory LGD) and false rejection 0.2644 (the
EMP-measure return parameter~\cite{verbraken2014}). A second pair from an
earlier training study (0.75/0.10) appears only in the sensitivity analyses
that cite it.

\subsection{A permutation audit for deployed routers}
The original production rule deferred on raw score disagreement
$|p_{ml}-p_{cbes}| > \delta$. We propose the following audit for any
deployed abstention rule. With $n_d$ deferrals and a deferred-pile statistic
$T$, draw $T_1,\dots,T_m$ from $m$ routers deferring $n_d$ uniformly random
cases and report both the standardised score
\begin{equation}
z \;=\; \frac{T - \bar{T}_{\mathrm{rand}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{rand}}}
\label{eq:audit}
\end{equation}
and the empirical permutation $p$-value
$p = (1 + \#\{T_i \text{ at least as extreme}\})/(m+1)$, one-sided in the
direction under test, with resolution floor $1/(m+1)$. A $z$-score alone can
be inflated by a small estimated null standard deviation, so we never
report one without its empirical $p$. The primary statistic is the
deferred-set decision loss
\begin{equation}
R_{\mathrm{defer}} = \tfrac{1}{|D|}\textstyle\sum_{i \in D}
\mathbb{1}\big[\hat{y}_i \neq y_i\big],
\label{eq:rdefer}
\end{equation}
where $D$ is the deferred set and $\hat{y}_i$ is the hard decision the
no-deferral engine would have taken at its own operating threshold. A
useful router should raise the deferred set's decision loss relative to
random routing. One sign convention holds throughout: the gate statistic
computes the deferred-pile accuracy $T = 1 - R_{\mathrm{defer}}$, the
one-sided alternative is lower-tail, and a useful router has negative $z$.
An anti-selective router (an easier-than-random pile) has positive $z$; its
$p$ is computed in the upper tail and marked ``inv.''\ wherever it appears.
Because 0/1 loss weights errors equally at an 8\% default rate, every audit
is accompanied by default recall among deferred cases and the expected
decision cost of the auto pile under the stated cost model.

The audit caught the deployed rule. At its historical operating point (it
deferred 51.8\% of cases, $m=200$) the deferred pile was far easier than
random ($z \approx +28$). Reconstructed at the matched 22.5\% capacity rate
and re-audited with $m = 10{,}000$, the disagreement rule routes fewer
defaulters to review than random deferral would (16.5\% against the 22.5\%
random expectation), and no random router among 10{,}000 produced a pile as
easy ($z = +36.0$; empirical $p < 10^{-4}$, inverted direction). The rule
was systematically sending the model's most confident cases to humans.
Fig.~\ref{fig:auditnull} shows both null distributions. The point is not
that this particular rule was foolish; it is that a plausible-looking rule
inverted silently, and no aggregate metric showed it.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_audit_null.pdf}
\caption{The audit of Eq.~\eqref{eq:audit} with $m=10{,}000$ random routers,
both routers at the matched 22.5\% rate. Top: the disagreement router's
deferred pile is easier than any random draw (inverted). Bottom: the
repaired uncertainty router's pile is harder than any random draw. Neither
observed value is reachable by chance at the $10^{-4}$ resolution.}
\label{fig:auditnull}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Diagnosis}
Measured on the full out-of-fold population, the two scores differ by a
near-constant calibration offset: mean $p_{ml} - p_{cbes} = +0.307$,
positive on 98.4\% of rows. Removing the constant offset shrinks the mean
disagreement magnitude by roughly two thirds, and the residual correlates
positively with model confidence ($r = 0.38$), so thresholding
$|p_{ml}-p_{cbes}|$ preferentially defers confident cases. The general
lesson: a disagreement signal between two differently calibrated scores
measures their scales before it measures difficulty.

\subsection{Repair: racing candidate signals at matched capacity}
We raced candidate signals at the mandated 22.5\% rate, all thresholds
fitted on the tuning half only, all audited on the held-out half with
$m=10{,}000$ (Table~\ref{tab:audit}; serving frame, held-out half of
population C). Normalising the disagreement signal's scales before
differencing (rank, z-score, or isotonic calibration) fixes the sign. The
repair we deployed is plain model uncertainty, the distance of $p_{ml}$
from the operating threshold: it raises default recall in review to 24.7\%
and lowers the auto-pile cost from 0.0731 with no deferral to 0.0484 per
applicant ($z = -59.7$, $p < 10^{-4}$), stable across tune/test re-splits
($z = -59.7 / -58.8 / -63.1$ over three split seeds). The
$|p_{ml}-0.5|$ variant posts the largest statistics (57.3\% recall;
$z = -263.1$) because, with nearly all scores above 0.5, it reduces to
deferring the lowest-scoring band. That is a risk ordering, and it largely
defers cases the engine would auto-reject, so we report it and do not
deploy it; the audit exists to make exactly this choice visible. The
decision artifact's band policy is near-random at isolating difficulty
($z = -0.9$, $p = 0.19$): no longer inverted, but difficulty-targeted
signals do strictly better.

A sensitivity sweep recomputes Table~\ref{tab:audit}'s cost column under
both project cost pairs and ratios 2--20. The qualitative conclusions do
not move: the disagreement rule is last or next-to-last under every
assumption, and the margin rule is in the top three everywhere (first at
ratios $\geq$10). Which uncertainty variant is cheapest depends on the
assumed loss ratio, so the ranking is reported per assumption.

\subsection{A selection-bias-free confirmation}\label{sec:finaltest}
Racing six candidates and quoting the winner from the same held-out half
uses that half for model selection. We therefore repeated the exercise
under a three-stage design: 50\% TUNE (all signal fitting and thresholds),
25\% SELECTION (the race, winner picked by a rule fixed before results:
highest deferred-pile loss inside the rate band), and an untouched 25\%
FINAL slice evaluated once. The selection slice picks the $|p_{ml}{-}0.5|$
variant, and the final slice confirms it: 56.8\% of the slice's defaulters
routed to review and auto-pile cost 0.0253 against 0.0729 with no deferral
($z = -186.3$, $p < 10^{-4}$). The margin rule constitutes a second
pre-specified router on this slice (fixed by a dated commit before the
present decision artifact existed) and also confirms: cost 0.0482
($z = -42.7$, $p < 10^{-4}$). The band policy remains near-random
($z = -0.5$, $p = 0.30$). The selection rule picks the risk-ordering
variant and we still deploy the margin rule: the selection criterion
rewards raw pile difficulty, and we weigh difficulty against deferring
cases the engine would reject anyway; both candidates are confirmed on the
final slice, so the choice between them is a stated policy decision rather
than a statistical one.

\subsection{Routing on epistemic uncertainty}
Beyond the repair, we evaluated epistemic uncertainty from a single
SGLB-trained CatBoost (posterior-sampling mode; $K{=}10$ virtual
ensembles~\cite{ustimenko2021,malinin2021}). SGLB's Langevin noise makes
the boosting trajectory sample from a posterior over ensembles, so
truncating one trained model at staggered iteration counts yields $K$
approximate posterior members without training $K$ models. With member
probabilities $p_1,\dots,p_K$ and $\bar{p} = \tfrac{1}{K}\sum_k p_k$,
\begin{equation}
\underbrace{\mathcal{H}(\bar{p})}_{\text{total}} \;=\;
\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{K}\textstyle\sum_k \mathcal{H}(p_k)}_{\text{data (aleatoric)}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{know}}}_{\text{knowledge (epistemic)}} ,
\label{eq:decomp}
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{H}$ is binary entropy and the mutual-information residual
$\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{know}}$ is the deferral signal. At an 8\% base rate
nearly all predictions sit below 0.5, making total and data entropy
near-monotone in $\bar{p}$ (correlation 0.94); knowledge uncertainty is the
only component not reducible to the score (correlation $-0.36$ with the
reject-option signal), which is why it carries routing information the
reject-option rule cannot see. We summarise routing quality by the
random-to-oracle position
$(R_{\mathrm{rand}} - R_{\mathrm{sel}})/(R_{\mathrm{rand}} -
R_{\mathrm{oracle}})$: 0 means the kept-pile error rate (the selective
risk) is what a random router leaves, 1 means it is the best achievable
when the actual errors are deferred first. These SGLB results are in the
research operating frame (the model's own Youden threshold), so their
absolute risks are not comparable with the serving-frame costs of
Table~\ref{tab:audit}. At the matched rate on the test half
(Fig.~\ref{fig:riskcov}), knowledge uncertainty reached position 0.40
against 0.14 for the reject-option baseline~\cite{chow1970} (selective risk
0.217 against 0.271; random 0.299), approaching a two-model disagreement
signal (0.47) without a second model. It is also higher on thin-file
applicants, as an epistemic signal should be.

The signal predicts error, which is what a routing signal must do. Binned
by tune-split deciles of knowledge uncertainty, the test-half
decision-error rate rises monotonically from 5.0\% in the lowest decile to
64.7\% in the highest (error-detection AUROC 0.749; overall error rate
29.9\%; Fig.~\ref{fig:deciles}). The reject-option margin scored the same
way sits below chance (AUROC 0.462) because at this base rate its smallest
margins concentrate in the risky band the engine already rejects.

The result is not an artifact of $K$ or of one training run. Across
$K \in \{5, 10, 20, 50\}$ and three training-seed sets (twelve
configurations retrained under the full protocol), the random-to-oracle
position stays within 0.37--0.40 and the OOF AUC within 0.7745--0.7750.
One caveat: within a seed the per-case uncertainty ranks are insensitive to
$K$ (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.99$), but across training seeds they correlate
at $\rho \approx 0.68$, so individual routing decisions are moderately
run-dependent even though aggregate quality is not; a production promotion
should average uncertainties over seeds.

\subsection{Uncertainty against expected loss}\label{sec:costaware}
Uncertainty is not financial risk: a model can be uncertain about an
economically small case and confidently wrong about an expensive one. We
raced routing objectives across a review-capacity grid
(Fig.~\ref{fig:frontier}), under the same three-stage discipline as
Sec.~\ref{sec:finaltest}: random; the reject-option margin; knowledge
uncertainty; expected decision cost
$\mathbb{E}[L_i] = p_i c_{FA}$ for auto-approvals and $(1-p_i)c_{FR}$ for
auto-rejections; and a rank-blend of knowledge uncertainty and expected
loss with the mixing weight chosen on the selection slice. The selection
slice chooses $\lambda^{*} = 0$, pure expected-cost ranking. This is a
negative result for our headline signal on the cost criterion. At the
22.5\% rate on the final slice (research frame), expected-cost ranking
leaves an auto-pile cost of 0.0314 per applicant (95\% CI
$[0.0308, 0.0320]$) against 0.0479 for knowledge uncertainty, 0.0583 for
the margin rule and 0.0831 with no deferral. Uncertainty and economic risk
are different routing objectives: epistemic uncertainty buys error
isolation, expected-loss ranking buys cost reduction, and an institution
should pick and audit the objective it actually holds its review capacity
for. The result is wired as well as reported: the serving engine exposes
expected-loss routing as a third flag-gated mode, calibrated in the serving
frame under the same tune/test discipline (at the matched 22.5\% rate the
auto-pile cost falls $0.0731 \to 0.0291$ per auto-decided applicant and
42.0\% of defaulters reach review, against 24.7\% under the default margin
rule). The margin rule is the production default; promoting the
expected-loss mode is the stated policy choice above.

\subsection{Who gets deferred}\label{sec:fairness}
Selective prediction can magnify group disparities~\cite{jones2021}, so a
deferral paper owes a subgroup account. We joined the decision artifact's
band policy to applicant attributes (gender, age, region rating,
bureau-file status) and measured the decision mix, ranking and calibration
per group. On attribute inputs: gender and age enter no component of the
decision pipeline; region is not in the 15-field serving contract but does
enter CBES's lowest-weight pillar, so a bounded region influence (at most
$\alpha \times 0.05$ of the blend) is present in every blended decision.
Review concentrates where information is missing: thin-file applicants are
deferred at 34.3\% against 20.5\% for documented applicants; their
auto-reject rate is also higher (39.0\% against 20.3\%), tracking their
higher observed default rate (10.1\% against 7.7\%). Decision-mix gaps
across gender (approval 59.1\% F against 45.7\% M) and age (36.7\% under 30
against 68.7\% over 60) track the groups' observed default rates (7.0\%
against 10.1\%; 11.5\% against 4.9\%) rather than deferral asymmetries
(deferral stays within 22.1--25.2\% across these groups). We report these
as measurements, not as a conditional-fairness analysis. Calibration is
tight in every group with $n \ge 500$ (10-bin ECE between 0.0011 and
0.0042) and ranking AUC spans 0.719--0.768.

The asymmetry depends on the router (Table~\ref{tab:subrouting}). The
inverted rule concentrated review on thin-file applicants at 3.4$\times$
the documented rate while capturing only 10.9\% of documented defaulters.
The band policy (1.7$\times$) carries a larger asymmetry than a random
router; the margin rule reduces it to 1.4$\times$; the epistemic router is
nearly flat (24.4\% against 22.4\%) while giving thin-file applicants the
highest default recall of any comparable policy. The reduction is not
monotonic across policies, and whether extra thin-file review helps those
applicants depends on reviewer behaviour we have not measured. This is a
descriptive measurement of policies, not a regulatory fairness assessment.

\subsection{Stress tests and an independent-dataset replication}\label{sec:taiwan}
We subjected one SGLB model (trained on a 60\% slice, thresholds from a
20\% validation slice) to controlled corruptions of the remaining test
slice. These are synthetic stress tests, not evidence of real-world
generalisation. The monitoring quantity is free: the deferral rate at the
clean-fitted knowledge threshold, which a stable system should hold near
22.5\%. Under information loss (external-score and bureau columns masked
for a random half of rows) the rate rises to 56.6\% while AUC falls
$0.779 \to 0.720$ and 10-bin ECE rises $0.004 \to 0.053$. Under feature
noise (Gaussian, half a standard deviation, on 20\% of numeric columns)
accuracy is almost untouched (AUC 0.776) yet the rate rises to 38.4\%: the
signal reacts to distributional change before error moves. One negative
result: under a pure class-prior shift (default rate doubled by
subsampling) ranking is invariant (AUC 0.779) and calibration degrades
sharply (ECE 0.070), but knowledge uncertainty barely reacts (24.6\%);
prior shift belongs to calibration monitoring instead. In every scenario,
knowledge-routed deferral at the matched rate kept selective risk below the
scenario's overall error rate.

External validity cannot be argued from one corpus, so we replicated the
deferral layer end to end on the UCI Taiwan credit-card default
dataset~\cite{yeh2009} (30{,}000 real customers, 22.1\% default rate): same
fold seeds, same SGLB budget, same tune/test discipline, and the unmodified
Home Credit audit code. The replication confirms the machinery: SGLB trains
well (OOF AUC 0.7807), every uncertainty router beats random at the matched
22.5\% rate with the audit at its permutation floor ($p < 10^{-4}$ for all
three signals), and the knowledge deciles remain monotone in error (16.3\%
to 34.9\%). It also sharpens the signal choice: at Taiwan's 22\% base rate
the random-to-oracle ordering flips, with total uncertainty dominating
(position 0.415) over the reject-option margin (0.186) and knowledge
uncertainty (0.097). The mechanism is the one identified above: at an 8\%
prior, total entropy is near-reducible to the score and knowledge is the
only non-redundant component; at a 22\% prior that reduction no longer
holds. The portable conclusion is procedural: race candidate uncertainty
signals at your own operating prior and audit the winner. Importing a
routing signal untested, ours included, is the failure mode the audit is
there to catch.

\section{Supporting Results}\label{sec:results}
Two supporting studies explain why the deferral layer, and not a better
classifier, is where this system's decision quality improves. Full detail
is in the project's machine-readable reports.

\subsection{Features against fusion}
We held models, folds, and metric fixed and changed only the features: v1,
the original 113-column numeric frame; v2, 319 engineered columns adding
domain ratios, external-score combinations, and 35 aggregates of the
credit-bureau table. All twenty fold deltas are positive and every model's
mean gain is at least four times the noise floor (Fig.~\ref{fig:folddeltas});
a paired bootstrap on pooled out-of-fold predictions confirms the gains
(CatBoost $+0.0114$, 95\% CI $[0.0104, 0.0125]$; the bootstrap's v1
baseline is the slightly stronger production run, which is why its point
estimate is smaller than the fold-paired $+0.0155$). The best
like-for-like fusion of the improved models gains $+0.0016$, below the
claim floor, and out-of-fold correlations among the improved models remain
0.87--0.96: better features made every model better in the same way. A
14-configuration hyperparameter sweep improved the early-stopped default by
$+0.001$, and the capacity-adaptive learning curve still rises at full data
($+0.010$ AUC per doubling), so the remaining headroom was in information.
A second enrichment, 26 side-table aggregates designed before training and
judged by the identical rule, confirmed the prediction: CatBoost
$+0.0111$ and XGBoost $+0.0104$ fold-paired, every fold positive
(Table~\ref{tab:main}). Feature work moved the best model
$0.7603 \to 0.7868$ while every architectural change and fusion stayed
inside the noise floor.

\subsection{Foundation models and recent challengers}
Table~\ref{tab:fm} compares foundation models on population B: 8{,}000 rows
joined by applicant identity with an alignment gate (zero label mismatches),
a safeguard we recommend after an early row-misalignment incident. Both
foundation models trail the boosted baseline on the same rows; both fusions
fall under the claim floor, and averaging with TabFM lowers AUC
(CI $[-0.022, -0.007]$) despite TabFM being the most decorrelated partner
we tested ($\rho = 0.66$). Among recent challengers screened under the same
rules, RealMLP~\cite{holzmuller2024} lost every fold to CatBoost
($-0.0121$ fold-paired), and TabICLv2~\cite{qu2026} could not complete the
screen on commodity hardware (about 18\,GB of offload scratch per fold), a
deployability result in itself. Licensing narrows the field further: the
TabPFN-2.5 model card restricts commercial and production use of its model
outputs~\cite{tabpfn25}, so we evaluated that checkpoint for research
comparison only.

\section{Decision-Layer Studies}\label{sec:studies}
\textbf{The CBES blend, measured.} Because CBES is a decision signal and
not only an explanation layer (on the held-out half of population C it
ranks at AUC 0.5621 alone), we report the full decision mix the blend
changes, both configurations at the matched review rate. The blend costs
discrimination ($-0.0056$ AUC, paired-bootstrap CI $[-0.0067, -0.0045]$)
and raises rejected-or-deferred default capture from 75.1\% to 79.5\%. The
decomposition shows where the capture comes from: the blend converts
3{,}094 false approvals into 2{,}545 at the price of raising false
rejections from 26{,}967 to 28{,}314 (rejection rate 21.9\% $\to$ 23.1\%),
while default recall inside the deferred pile is nearly unchanged (21.6\%
$\to$ 22.0\%). Part of the capture gain is therefore rejecting more, and
the net expected cost depends on the loss ratio: under the main cost pair
the blend is slightly costlier per auto-decided applicant (0.0724 against
0.0716), while under the 7.5:1 pair of the training study below it is
cheaper (0.0398 against 0.0422). This is a measured decision-policy
trade-off; which side a lender takes is a policy choice over the loss
ratio, now priced.

\textbf{Monotonicity.} We fixed 21 sign constraints from domain knowledge
(external credit scores decrease risk; payment burden, bureau overdues,
leverage and prolongations increase it; demographic fields deliberately
unconstrained) and retrained the best model under them. Fold-paired cost:
$-0.0008$ AUC, inside the claim floor, with zero direction violations in
14{,}400 sampled sweep checks. The constraint holds by construction for
each listed feature with the other inputs held fixed; the checks are
sampled verification, not an exhaustive proof. Within that scope,
directional adverse-action explanations become model properties, which
post-hoc attribution alone cannot guarantee.

\textbf{Cost-sensitive training.} With the training study's stated 7.5:1
cost model, class-weighted training never beat cost-optimal thresholding of
the unweighted model (test cost delta $+0.000087$ per applicant;
paired-bootstrap CI spans zero; the weighted arm loses at four of five
decision-time cost ratios), confirming Elkan's analysis~\cite{elkan2001}
and justifying keeping the economics in auditable decision policy.

\section{Deployment and Governance}\label{sec:deploy}
CredDefer runs as a containerised cloud prototype (FastAPI backend, React
front-end) on commodity infrastructure defined end-to-end in Terraform; the
stack rebuilds from nothing in about 15 minutes and destroys to zero cost.
On the full population the engine's decision mix is 167{,}751 instant
approvals, 70{,}593 instant rejections and 69{,}167 deferrals (22.5\%);
reviewer adjudications flow through the same capture path, so the review
workflow is exercised end to end rather than mocked. The TabPFN-2.5 second
opinion is served from a free cloud GPU behind an authenticated tunnel,
consumed strictly as advisory input, and validated by a connection run that
scores 400 locally held labelled rows through four ordered gates
(configured; reachable; complete; recomputed AUC clears 0.60; last run
0.710). An LLM reviewer briefing summarises each deferred case under three
hard boundaries: advisory only, optional by construction, grounded in the
decision report with cited fields. No lending institution operates the
system, and claims about institutional adoption are out of scope. We map
these mechanisms to the explainability, human-oversight and
model-governance expectations of the RBI Digital Lending
Directions~\cite{rbi2025} and the FREE-AI report~\cite{rbifreeai} in the
project documentation; the mapping is a technical alignment produced by the
authors, not a compliance assessment.

\section{Limitations}
Our primary results come from one dataset, with Indian-market regulatory
framing over non-Indian data and literature cost parameters rather than
measured ones. The corpus carries no timestamps, so real temporal shift is
untestable here; the stress tests are controlled synthetic corruptions. The
independent-dataset replication covers the deferral layer only; the
feature, serving and subgroup results remain single-corpus, and the
replication showed the routing-signal choice to be base-rate dependent, so
no fixed signal should be transported without racing it again at the new
prior. The serving/research accuracy gap (0.6919 against 0.7868) reflects
the deliberate 15-field serve-time contract not yet extended to the
engineered features; the numbers come from different populations and
feature frames. Deferral findings are reported in two operating frames
(serving and research) whose baselines differ; the SGLB routing result
awaits production promotion. We compare against no trained
learning-to-defer or conformal baseline; adding one under the same budget
is left as an author decision. The review workflow is a deployed prototype
with outcome capture; we conducted no human-subject evaluation, so claims
about human-AI complementarity are out of scope. The subgroup analysis is
descriptive, not causal. All cost conclusions are conditional on the stated
cost pairs; the three-stage final slice comes from the same corpus, so it
removes selection bias but not single-dataset risk; and per-case epistemic
ranks vary across training seeds ($\rho \approx 0.68$) even though
aggregate routing quality does not.

\section{Conclusion}
Treating the decision pipeline, rather than the classifier, as the research
object yielded findings a leaderboard cannot express. A deployed deferral
rule had silently inverted; a cheap permutation test caught it, the
diagnosis explained it, and the repair survived an untouched final split
and now runs as the production default. A single boosted model supplies
epistemic routing without an ensemble, robustly across ensemble sizes and
training seeds. Uncertainty and economic risk are different routing
objectives, and expected-loss ranking minimises decision cost at fixed
capacity. The subgroup footprint of deferral is a property of the router.
Accuracy headroom on this corpus lives in the features, and a
regulator-relevant explainability guarantee costs an AUC delta inside the
noise floor. The deferral layer replicates on an independent corpus, where
the audit transports and the best uncertainty signal shifts with the base
rate. The procedure, not the signal, is the portable artifact: audit any
deployed abstention rule against a random-router null, report effect sizes
with empirical $p$-values, and race candidate signals at your own operating
prior. Future work: a learned-deferral or conformal baseline under the
same budget; full-system replication on an independent portfolio; temporal
aggregates of the credit-history tables; promotion of the
engineered-feature model behind the serving contract; and a human-subject
evaluation of the review workflow.

every number above traces to one. Protocols were fixed in advance and
committed with timestamps: the features-against-fusion protocol (commit
\texttt{8bd7cbf}, 2026-09-23), the three model-modification studies
(\texttt{4a7cb4c}, 2026-09-30) and the deferral race (\texttt{0a253bd},
2026-08-31) carry their claim rules in the script headers, committed before
results were generated. The revision studies (the 10{,}000-permutation
audit, the three-stage final-test split, the SGLB robustness sweep, the
cost-aware routing comparison and the subgroup routing comparison) are
likewise committed scripts with their selection rules stated in their
headers. Code, infrastructure definitions, figure generators,
machine-readable reports, dependency versions and seeds are prepared for
release as a public archive; the Home Credit licence does not permit
redistributing derived row-level data, so the archive ships regeneration
scripts for all artifacts instead of the artifacts themselves.
